summary: Specifies the Trivial File Transfer Protocol, a very simple protocol for moving files between hosts. This second revision was later replaced. Replaced by RFC 1350.

plainLanguage.summary: TFTP is a simple protocol for reading or writing a file on another host. It sends one block at a time and waits for an acknowledgment, and RFC 783 was later replaced by RFC 1350.

questions: when to use tftp instead of ftp
how does tftp transfer a file
subtitle: A minimal request-and-reply protocol for copying files between hosts

tldr.problem: Hosts needed a small, simple way to transfer files across networks that support datagram delivery.
tldr.mechanism: TFTP sends a read or write request, then transfers numbered data blocks. Each block is acknowledged before the next is sent.
tldr.outcome: The revision was later replaced by RFC 1350.

sections.title: Purpose and Design
sections.content:
The Trivial File Transfer Protocol (TFTP) is designed to be small and easy to implement. This revision describes moving files between machines using UDP, though the RFC says other datagram protocols are also possible.

TFTP can read and write files, or send mail in its mail mode. It does not list directories or provide user authentication. Its restrictions simplify implementation.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP keeps file transfer simple: it can read or write a named file, but it does not list folders or check who the user is. This version describes using UDP to carry its messages.

sections.title: Starting and Completing a Transfer
sections.content:
A transfer begins with a read request (RRQ) or write request (WRQ). The request also asks to open a connection. Each side chooses a transfer identifier (TID), which is passed to the datagram protocol as a port; the initial request goes to the server's well-known TID 69.

Once accepted, the transfer uses numbered data blocks. A receiver acknowledges each block before the sender sends the next. A short final data block marks the end; errors are reported with an ERROR packet, which is not itself acknowledged or retransmitted.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks to read or write a file, and the server answers with data or an acknowledgment. They exchange one block at a time; a block shorter than 512 bytes marks the end of the file.

sections.title: Packets and Transfer Modes
sections.content:
Every TFTP packet begins with a two-byte opcode. The five packet types are RRQ, WRQ, DATA, ACK and ERROR. Data packets include a block number and zero to 512 bytes of data; acknowledgment packets echo the block number.

Requests name a file and a mode. Netascii represents text, octet transfers raw eight-bit bytes, and mail sends netascii characters to a recipient instead of a file. Other modes may be agreed between cooperating hosts, but the RFC assigns no central authority to name them.
sections.plainLanguage: TFTP has packets for requests, data, acknowledgments and errors. A request selects text conversion, unchanged eight-bit data, or mail delivery; each data packet carries a block number.

references.text: Postel, J., "User Datagram Protocol," RFC 768, August 28, 1980.
